A year after Claude Code creator Boris Cherny began relying on AI to write all his code, he’s looking to eliminate the time he spends waiting for someone to approve it.

In a post on X on Monday, Cherny described how pull request workflows haven’t kept pace with the speed of AI-assisted development.

Under certain repository configurations, AI-generated code could now merge without human review.

Anthropic’s approach could fundamentally change how engineering teams govern software delivery. Under certain repository configurations, AI-generated code could now merge without human review.

Shipping without human review

The mechanics behind Claude Ship, which Anthropic introduced for Team and Enterprise customers, reveal how the company intends to address a bottleneck that its own coding agents have helped create. Instead of asking engineers to approve every change, Anthropic wants them to decide upfront which changes need a human review.

From writing code to shipping it

The company has been wrestling with the review bottleneck internally for months. Between June and September, the number of merged PRs in the Claude Code codebase more than doubled, while the proportion that required a revert fell by more than 40%, according to an October engineering blog post by Anthropic’s technical staff, Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang.

“We didn’t remove review,” the engineers wrote. Much of the work previously done by human reviewers had shifted to machines, alongside investments in infrastructure that made it easier to reverse problematic changes.

Claude Ship extends that approach beyond Anthropic’s existing multi-agent Code Review tool. PR Steward addresses issues that prevent a pull request from moving forward, while Claude Approvals determines whether the proposed changes satisfy the repository’s approval policy. Both new agents are in beta.

Developers can start the process with the /ship command in Claude Code. If administrators enable Claude Ship for a repository, PR Steward can push commits to address feedback from human or automated reviewers without waiting for a developer to initiate the process. Existing repository rules and permissions still apply.

Defining what needs approval

Claude Approvals supports natural-language classifiers and Code Review findings in repository-level policies that determine which changes require human approval.

With GitHub’s auto-merge enabled and repository rules permitting automated approval, Claude-approved changes can reach the default branch without human review once all required checks and other merge requirements are satisfied.

More sensitive changes still require one or two human approvals, neither of which an agent can satisfy.

At Anthropic, certain low-risk changes can already ship without human approval if they pass automated review and security checks. More sensitive changes still require one or two human approvals, neither of which an agent can satisfy.

Lessons from Code Review’s development

During the internal development of Code Review, before Claude Ship launched, Anthropic encountered a problem with automated review. As detailed in its October engineering blog post, an internal CLI pull request went through more than 50 rounds of review and remediation overnight before its author intervened.

“Review has to converge,” the engineering team wrote.

The engineering team subsequently limited its internal review process to three rounds before asking the author to reconsider the implementation. It also narrowed the scope of subsequent reviews and introduced measures to reduce repetitive findings.

Anthropic tells T he New Stack that Claude Ship incorporates the fix and caps automated reviews at three rounds.

Anthropic tells T he New Stack that Claude Ship incorporates the fix and caps automated reviews at three rounds.

What automated review costs

When Anthropic introduced Code Review in March, the company estimated that reviews would typically cost between $15 and $25, depending on the size and complexity of the pull request.

Claude Ship introduces additional inference costs when agents work to resolve outstanding pull request issues. Administrators can configure review depths and spending limits for the relevant tools.

Correction: An earlier version of this article incorrectly attributed a review loop that ran for more than 50 rounds to Claude Ship. The incident occurred during Anthropic’s internal development of Code Review, before Claude Ship launched.
